title: Why does a random UUIDv4 primary key hurt write performance (B-tree page splits, index bloat, worse on InnoDB), and how do you fix it with UUIDv7, ULID, or a sequential id?
shortTitle: Why does random UUID primary key hurt performance?

s1_definition.profdef: A random UUID version 4 is 122 random bits with no ordering. When used as a primary-key index, each new insert lands at a RANDOM position in the B-tree index rather than appending at the end. This causes B-TREE PAGE SPLITS (a full page must split to make room in the middle), INDEX FRAGMENTATION (pages end up half-full and scattered), poor BUFFER-POOL/CACHE locality (every insert touches a different page, so the working set does not fit in memory), and larger index size on disk. It is WORSE on MySQL InnoDB because InnoDB uses a CLUSTERED index: the primary key physically orders the table rows, so random primary keys scatter the ACTUAL ROW DATA, not just a secondary index — and every secondary index stores the full primary key, so a 16-byte random UUID bloats every index. The fix is a TIME-ORDERED identifier: UUIDv7 (timestamp-prefixed UUID), ULID (lexicographically sortable), or a plain sequential bigint — inserts then append near the end of the index, avoiding splits and keeping the hot pages cache-resident.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India files transactions in a giant sorted ledger. A sequential id is like filing each new transaction at the BACK of the book — quick, the last page is always open on the desk. A random UUIDv4 is like being told to insert each new transaction at a RANDOM page in the middle; the clerk constantly has to shove existing entries aside to make room (page split), the book becomes full of half-empty pages (fragmentation), and the clerk must keep fetching different pages from the archive instead of keeping one open page handy (cache misses). A time-ordered id like UUIDv7 puts the new entries near the back again, so filing is fast once more.
s1_definition.oneliner: Random UUIDv4 as a PK scatters inserts across the B-tree causing page splits, fragmentation, and cache misses — and worst on InnoDB's clustered index where the PK orders the rows themselves; fix with a time-ordered id (UUIDv7, ULID, or sequential bigint) so inserts append.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A random UUID version 4 is 122 random bits with no ordering. When used as a primary-key index, each new insert lands at a RANDOM position in the B-tree index rather than appending at the end. This causes B-TREE PAGE SPLITS (a full page must split to make room in the middle), INDEX FRAGMENTATION (pages end up half-full and scattered), poor BUFFER-POOL/CACHE locality (every insert touches a different page, so the working set does not fit in memory), and larger index size on disk. It is WORSE on MySQL InnoDB because InnoDB uses a CLUSTERED index: the primary key physically orders the table rows, so random primary keys scatter the ACTUAL ROW DATA, not just a secondary index — and every secondary index stores the full primary key, so a 16-byte random UUID bloats every index. The fix is a TIME-ORDERED identifier: UUIDv7 (timestamp-prefixed UUID), ULID (lexicographically sortable), or a plain sequential bigint — inserts then append near the end of the index, avoiding splits and keeping the hot pages cache-resident.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India files transactions in a giant sorted ledger. A sequential id is like filing each new transaction at the BACK of the book — quick, the last page is always open on the desk. A random UUIDv4 is like being told to insert each new transaction at a RANDOM page in the middle; the clerk constantly has to shove existing entries aside to make room (page split), the book becomes full of half-empty pages (fragmentation), and the clerk must keep fetching different pages from the archive instead of keeping one open page handy (cache misses). A time-ordered id like UUIDv7 puts the new entries near the back again, so filing is fast once more.

**One line to remember:** Random UUIDv4 as a PK scatters inserts across the B-tree causing page splits, fragmentation, and cache misses — and worst on InnoDB's clustered index where the PK orders the rows themselves; fix with a time-ordered id (UUIDv7, ULID, or sequential bigint) so inserts append.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the production incident at National Bank of India that taught the team this lesson.

Problem 1 — insert throughput collapsed as the transactions table grew. A new ledger service used a random UUIDv4 as the primary key of the `transactions` table. In testing with a small table it was fine, but in production, once the table grew past the buffer pool size, insert latency climbed sharply and the nightly batch overran its window. This is exactly the random-UUID cache-thrash and page-split problem: every insert targeted a random page that had to be fetched from disk and often split.

Problem 2 — the index was far larger than expected. Monitoring showed the primary-key index on disk was almost double the size of the data it held. This is exactly index fragmentation from page splits leaving pages half-full.

Problem 3 — it was especially bad because the team planned to move to MySQL InnoDB. On InnoDB the primary key is clustered, so the random UUID would have scattered the row data itself and bloated every secondary index with a 16-byte key. This is exactly why the fix had to come before that migration.

The fix recorded in the project: switch the clustered/primary key to a time-ordered id. The team chose UUIDv7 so they kept a globally-unique, application-generatable id for their distributed ledger nodes, but one whose high bits encode time so inserts append near the end of the index. For an internal-only table they used a sequential bigint instead.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `LedgerTransaction` entity whose primary key uses a TIME-ORDERED UUID (UUIDv7-style via Hibernate's time-based UUID generator), with a clear comment contrasting it against the random v4 that caused the problem. There is a `LedgerService`, annotated `@Transactional`, that inserts a batch of transactions and logs that the ids are time-ordered (so they sort roughly by insertion time). A small utility demonstrates the ordering difference by comparing a sequence of generated time-ordered ids against random ones. A test verifies that time-ordered ids generated in sequence are monotonically increasing when compared as strings, while random v4 ids are not.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is recording one hundred ledger transactions for Rajesh's account, and generating ids to show the ordering difference.

Step 1: `recordBatch("SAV2001", 100)` runs in a `@Transactional` method and builds one hundred transient `LedgerTransaction` objects.

Step 2: Each entity's primary key is generated by the time-ordered UUID generator (UUIDv7-style). The high bits encode the current millisecond timestamp, so an id generated now sorts AFTER one generated a moment ago. Because the id is known before flush, Hibernate can also batch the inserts.

Step 3: On save, Hibernate issues the INSERTs. In the primary-key B-tree index, each new id is larger (as sorted bytes) than the previous ones, so every insert lands on the RIGHTMOST leaf page. That page stays hot in the buffer pool, fills neatly, and only occasionally allocates a fresh page at the end. There are no mid-tree page splits and no fragmentation.

Step 4: Contrast the random-v4 path, shown by the ordering demo. A random v4 id has no relation to time, so a freshly generated value might sort anywhere in the index. Inserting it forces the database to find a random leaf page, possibly split it, and fetch it from disk if it is not cached. Over a large table this produces half-full pages (bloat) and constant cache misses (thrash), collapsing insert throughput.

Step 5: The ordering demo generates a handful of time-ordered ids with a small delay and confirms they come out already sorted — proving they would append in the index. It then generates random v4 ids and confirms they are NOT sorted — proving they would scatter. The report returns both lists and the note explaining the consequence for the B-tree.

```
2026-10-24 00:48:03 INFO  LedgerService - Recorded 100 txns for SAV2001 — time-ordered PKs append (no fragmentation)
2026-10-24 00:48:03 FINE  LedgerService - batched INSERTs; ids monotonic → rightmost leaf page stays hot
2026-10-24 00:48:03 INFO  LedgerService - Time-ordered ids sorted-as-generated=true ; random v4 sorted=false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ RANDOM UUIDv4 PK (the problem) ═══

  insert id=3f2a..  → B-tree: lands in the MIDDLE
    │ target leaf page full → PAGE SPLIT (allocate + move half the rows)
    │ pages left ~50% full → INDEX FRAGMENTATION (index ~2× data size)
    │ each insert touches a DIFFERENT page → fetched from disk → CACHE THRASH
    ▼
  InnoDB (worse): PK is CLUSTERED
    │ random PK scatters the ROW DATA itself (not just an index)
    │ every secondary index stores the full 16-byte PK → all indexes bloat
    ▼
  throughput collapses once table > buffer pool

  ═══ TIME-ORDERED ID (the fix) ═══

  insert id=01H...  (UUIDv7: timestamp high bits) → B-tree: lands at the END
    │ rightmost leaf page stays HOT in buffer pool
    │ fills neatly → new page appended only when full → NO mid-tree splits
    │ few pages touched → cache-resident → fast inserts even on huge tables
    ▼
  options:
    UUIDv7     → time-ordered + globally unique + app/distributed generatable
    ULID       → 128-bit, lexicographically sortable, compact base-32 text
    bigint seq → smallest/fastest when distribution not required

  ═══ ADVANCED PATTERN ═══
  internal clustered PK = sequential bigint (fast storage)
  external public id     = random UUID with its own index (non-guessable)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A random UUID version 4 has no ordering, so when it is used as a primary-key index every insert lands at a random position in the B-tree rather than appending at the end. That causes page splits, because a full leaf page in the middle must split and move half its rows to make room; it causes index fragmentation, because those split pages end up half full so the index grows far larger than the data; and it causes cache thrash, because each insert touches a different page that must be fetched from disk, so once the table outgrows the buffer pool insert throughput collapses. It is worst on MySQL InnoDB because InnoDB uses a clustered index where the primary key physically orders the row data itself, so a random primary key scatters the actual rows, and because every secondary index stores the full primary key, a sixteen-byte random UUID bloats every index.

The fix is a time-ordered identifier so inserts append near the end of the index while staying globally unique. UUIDv7 encodes a millisecond timestamp in the high bits followed by random bits, so values sort in roughly insertion order; ULID is a sortable timestamp-prefixed id with a compact text form; and a plain sequential bigint is the smallest and fastest when I do not need distributed generation. In our ledger service at National Bank of India, the transactions table originally used a random v4 primary key and insert latency climbed and the index bloated to nearly double the data size as the table grew, which would have been even worse on our planned InnoDB migration. We switched the clustered key to UUIDv7, which kept a globally-unique, application-generatable id for our distributed ledger nodes but made inserts append again.

The senior nuance I add is that if I need a random, non-guessable identifier for external exposure, I keep a sequential bigint or a UUIDv7 as the internal clustered primary key for storage efficiency and expose a separate random UUID as the public id with its own index. That way I get fast append-friendly inserts internally and non-sequential, non-guessable ids externally, instead of paying the fragmentation cost of a random clustered key.
